3.55.m: Vyāsa said: / One should not injure any living beings, nor ever speak an untruth; / one should not speak what is harmful or unpleasant, nor ever be a thief.
Whether grass or vegetable, earth or even water, / taking what belongs to another, a creature goes to hell.
One should not accept gifts from a king, nor from a Śūdra or a fallen man, / nor from any other [unworthy source]; if one is able, the wise man should avoid censured people.
One should not become a constant beggar, nor should one beg repeatedly from that same person; / begging thus, the beggar takes away the life-breaths of that foolish man.
One should not steal the property of the gods, especially a best of twice-born; / nor should one take the property of a Brahmin, even in times of distress.
They say that poison is not [true] poison; the property of a Brahmin is said to be poison. / Therefore, one should also carefully avoid the property of the gods at all times.
Flowers, vegetables, water, wood, and likewise roots, fruits, and grass— / Manu Prajāpati declared that taking these unoffered is not theft.
A twice-born man may take flowers for the rite of worshipping the deity, / but not continuously from a single person without permission.
The wise man may take grass, wood, fruits, and flowers openly; / they say it is only for the sake of dharma; otherwise, he becomes fallen.
A handful of sesame, mung beans, barley, and the like may be taken by those on a journey / who are hungry, not otherwise, O Brahmins; such is the rule set by the laws and other authorities.
One should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma after committing a sin, / concealing the sin by means of the vow and deceiving women and Śūdras.
Such a Brahmin is censured here and in the hereafter by the knowers of the Veda; / and whatever vow is performed deceitfully goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, having no religious marks, adopts a livelihood disguised in the dress of one who has them, / takes upon himself the sin of those who possess the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
Constantly begging, establishing marriage alliances, living together, and conversing [with the fallen] / causes one to fall; therefore, one should avoid them with effort.
One should not act with hostility toward the gods, nor likewise toward the guru; / hostility toward the guru is millions of times worse than hostility toward the gods.
Public censure and atheism are millions of times worse than that. / By cattle, by deities, by Brahmins, by agriculture, and by service to the king,
families that are deficient in dharma sink into ignominy, / through bad opinions, through neglect of rituals, and through non-recitation of the Vedas,
and through disrespecting Brahmins, families sink into ignominy; / through untruth, through adultery, and likewise through eating forbidden food,
and through conduct contrary to the family's dharma, a family is quickly destroyed; / and through giving gifts to those who are not learned in the Veda and likewise to outcasts,
and to those devoid of prescribed conduct, a family is quickly destroyed. / One should not live in a village surrounded by unrighteous people or abundant in disease,
nor should one live in a realm ruled by a Śūdra, nor one surrounded by heretics. / The auspicious region between the Himālaya and the Vindhya mountains, between the eastern and western
oceans—excepting that region, a twice-born man should not dwell anywhere else; / or where the black antelope roams naturally at all times,
or where holy, renowned rivers flow, there a twice-born man may dwell. / Avoiding half a krośa from the riverbank, a best of twice-born
should not reside anywhere else [that is not] sacred, nor near a settlement of outcasts; / nor should one dwell with fallen persons, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas,
nor with fools, nor with the haughty, nor with any actors and dancers. / A common bed, a seat, sitting in the same row, mixing cooked food in one pot,
offering sacrifices, teaching, marriage alliances, and likewise eating together, / studying together as the tenth, and officiating at sacrifices together—
these eleven are declared to be faults leading to confusion of caste. / Even by remaining in proximity, sin is transmitted to men;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid confusion of caste. / When seated in a single row, if they do not touch one another
because a boundary has been made with ashes, there is no confusion among them. / By fire, by ashes, by water, by a line drawn,
by a doorway, or by a pathway between pillars—by these six a row is divided. / One should not engage in pointless enmities, nor in disputes, nor in slander.
One should never report a cow grazing in another's field; / one should not dwell with an informer, nor strike anyone at a vulnerable spot.
A wise man should not describe to another a halo around the sun, nor an afternoon rainbow, / nor the moon, nor gold.
One should not enter into conflict with many, nor likewise with kinsmen; / what is displeasing to oneself, one should not practice upon others.
One should not announce the lunar day of the fortnight, nor point out constellations; / a best of twice-born should not converse with a menstruating woman, nor with an impure person.
One should not hinder what is being given to gods, gurus, and Brahmins; / one should not praise oneself, and one should avoid censuring others.
One should carefully avoid reviling the Vedas and reviling the gods. / But whatever twice-born man reviles the gods, the sages, or the Vedas,
no expiation is seen for him in the scriptures, O lords of sages! / If one should revile a guru, a god, or the Veda along with its supplements,
that man is cooked in Raurava for a full hundred million kalpas. / In the presence of reviling, one should remain silent and speak no answer at all;
covering one's ears, one should walk away, and one should not look at him. / A wise man should avoid secrets and the condemnation of others.
One should never engage in dispute with one's own kin; / a best of twice-born should not speak evil of sinners, nor [speak of them as] sinless.
By telling the truth, the fault would be equal; by falsehood, he would become guilty of sin. / The tears shed from weeping by men who are falsely accused
destroy the sons and cattle of those false accusers. / For the murder of a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and intercourse with the guru's wife,
purification has indeed been seen by the elders; there is none for false accusation. / One should not look at the rising sun, or at the moon, without a reason,
nor at it setting, nor in water, nor eclipsed, nor at midday; / one should not look at it concealed, nor as reflected in a mirror and the like.
One should never look upon a naked woman or man, / nor upon urine or feces, nor upon those engaged in sexual intercourse.
Being impure, the wise man should not look at the sun, the moon, and other planets; / he should not speak to another when he is ucchiṣṭa or covered with a veil.
One should not watch the touching of a corpse, nor look upon the face of an angry guru, / nor one's reflection in oil or water, nor at a row [of diners] during a meal.
One should not look at an animal breaking loose from its tether, nor at an elephant in rut; / one should not eat together with one's wife, nor watch her eating,
or sneezing, or yawning, or sitting at her ease; / nor should one look at one's own form in water, whether attractive or unattractive.
The intelligent man should never leap across [auspicious objects] nor step upon them; / he should not give advice to a Śūdra, nor kṛsara, rice-milk, or curds,
nor leftover food, nor honey, ghee, a black antelope skin, or sacrificial offerings; / the wise man should not tell him a vow, nor speak of dharma to him.
And one should not come under the sway of anger; one should avoid hatred and passion, / greed, hypocrisy, deceit, malice, and reviling knowledge.
One should completely avoid envy, arrogance, grief, and delusion; / one should not cause distress to anyone, but one may strike a son or a pupil.
He should not associate with the low, nor should his mind ever be set on greed; / he should not despise himself, and he should diligently avoid humiliation.

A wise man should not show disrespect to an eminent person, nor make himself subject to latent impressions; / he should not scratch the earth with his nails, nor should he ever cause a cow to lie down.
Among rivers he should not speak ill of a river, nor among mountains of mountains; / neither in lodging nor at meals should he abandon a traveling companion.
He should not plunge naked into water, nor should he walk over fire; / he should not smear his body with oil left over from anointing his head.
He should not play with serpents or weapons; he should not touch his own apertures, / nor his secret hairs; and he should not travel with an uncultured person.
He should not indulge in restlessness of hands, feet, speech, or eyes; / nor in restlessness of the penis or belly, nor ever in that of the ears.
He should not make music with his limbs or nails, nor drink from his cupped hands; / he should never strike water with his feet or his hand.
He should not knock down roots and fruits with clods of earth; / he should not learn barbarian speech, nor should he drag a seat with his foot.
A wise man should not break his nails, crack his knuckles, cut, scratch, / or rub them uselessly without a cause.
He should not eat food placed in his lap, nor perform useless actions; / he should not dance, sing, or play musical instruments.
He should not scratch his head with both hands joined together; / he should not propitiate the gods with worldly praises, even if he were the master of speech.
He should not gamble with dice, nor run, nor pass feces or urine in water; / he should never go to sleep while impure from food, nor take a bath naked.
He should not recite while walking, nor touch his own head; / he should not bite his nails or hair with his teeth, nor wake a sleeping person.
He should not bask in the morning sun; he should avoid the smoke of a corpse; / he should not sleep in a deserted house, nor carry shoes himself.
He should not spit without a cause, nor cross a river with his arms; / he should never wash one foot with the other foot.
A wise man should not warm his feet in fire, nor wash them in a bronze vessel; / he should not stretch them out toward a deity, a brāhmaṇa, or a cow,
nor toward the wind, fire, a king, brāhmaṇas, the sun, or the moon. / Being impure, he should never sleep, drink, study, bathe, eat,
nor ever go outside. / Sleeping, studying, bathing, applying unctions, eating, walking—
these he should always avoid at both twilights and at midday. / When impure from food, a brāhmaṇa should not touch a cow, a brāhmaṇa, or fire with his hand;
nor should he move them with his foot, nor touch an image of a deity. / When impure, he should not attend on the fire, nor praise the gods or the sages.
He should not plunge into bottomless water, nor wash himself without a cause; / he should not drink water by drawing it up with his left hand or with his mouth directly.
He should not emerge without sipping water, nor discharge semen into water, / nor what is smeared with impurity, blood, or poisons.
He should not cross over a flowing stream [improperly], nor engage in sexual intercourse in water; / he should not cut down a sacred tree, nor spit into water.
He should never stand upon bones, ashes, skulls, / hair, thorns, chaff, charcoal, or dry cow dung.
A wise man should not step over fire, nor place it beneath himself anywhere; / a wise man should not place it at his feet, nor blow it with a winnowing basket.
He should not climb down a tree [carelessly], nor ever look around while impure; / he should not throw fire into fire, nor extinguish it with water.
He should not himself announce the death of a friend to others; / he should not offer unmerchantable goods or deceptive goods for sale.
A wise man should not blow a fire into flames with the breaths of his mouth while impure; / he should not cause the boundary to be moved at a holy site or a reservoir.
He should never break an agreement previously entered into; / he should not make beasts, tigers, or birds fight against one another.
He should not cause distress to others by means of water, wind, heat, and the like; / having caused elders to perform good deeds, he should not cheat them afterward.
In the evening and in the morning, he should bolt the house doors for protection. / Wearing garlands or perfumes outside, or eating together with one's wife,
or entering after engaging in a dispute—these he should avoid. / A brāhmaṇa should not stand while eating; a wise man should not chatter or laugh [while eating].
He should touch his own fire with his hand, but not remain long in water; / he should not blow it with a fan, nor with a winnowing basket or his hand.

He may kindle the fire with his mouth, for fire was born from the mouth. / A wise man should not converse with another man's wife, nor perform sacrifices for one for whom sacrifice should not be performed.
A brāhmaṇa should never wander alone, and he should avoid crowds; / he should never go to a temple [of a deity] without circumambulating it clockwise.
He should not wring out garments [there], nor sleep in a temple; / he should not set out on a journey alone, nor together with unrighteous people,
nor with those afflicted by disease, nor with śūdras, nor with an outcaste; / nor without shoes, nor lacking water and the like.
A twice-born man should never cross over a path or a funeral pyre; / he should not revile yogins, perfected beings, those under vows, or ascetics.
A wise man should not intentionally tread upon the shadow of a temple, / of the gods, of sacrificial patrons, of brāhmaṇas, or of a cow.
He should not let his own shadow be trodden upon by outcastes and the like, or by sick persons; / he should never stand upon charcoal, ashes, hair, and such things.
He should avoid the dust of a broom, and water from a bathing-cloth or a water pot; / a twice-born man should not eat inedible foods, nor drink what is not to be drunk.

3.56.m: Vyāsa said: / A brāhmaṇa should not eat the food of a śūdra out of delusion or desire; / he who eats it when there is no distress falls into the womb of a śūdra.
A twice-born man who eats the censured food of a śūdra for six months / becomes a śūdra even while living, and having died, he is born as a dog.
O best of sages, of a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra— / in whose belly the food remains when he dies, into that one's womb he goes.
The food of a king, the food of a quail-catcher, the food of a eunuch, of leather-workers, / the food of a multitude, and the food of a courtezan—these six foods he should avoid.
The food of oil-pressers, of washermen, of thieves, and of distillers, / the food of celestial musicians, of blacksmiths, and the food of one in mourning—these he should avoid.
The food of a potter, of a painter, of a usurer, and of an outcaste, / of the son of a remarried woman, of an umbrella-maker, and of an accused person,
of a goldsmith, of an actor, of a hunter, of a barren woman, of an invalid, / of a physician, of a promiscuous woman, and of an executioner,
the food of a thief, of an atheist, and of one who reviles deities, / the food of a seller of soma, and especially of a dog-cooker,
the food of a man henpecked by his wife, and of one in whose house is a paramour, / of an abandoned person, of a miser, and likewise of one who eats leavings,
the food of a sinner, the food of a multitude, and of one who lives by weapons, / the food of one who is frightened, of one weeping, food that has been cursed or mutilated,

food of an enemy of the sacred word, of one delighting in sin, food of an ancestor rite, food of one in mourning, / food of one who cooks for himself alone, food of a corpse-bearer, and of an invalid,
food of childless women, and likewise of an ungrateful person, / especially the food of an artisan, and of a seller of weapons,

the food of a liquor-maker, the food of a bell-ringer, and the food of healers, / the food of an adulterous lover of a learned woman's husband, and the food of a younger brother who married before his elder.
[Food] of a remarried woman, especially, and of the husband of a remarried woman; / [food] given with disrespect, food shaken off, [given] with anger, or accompanied by astonishment;
even the food of a guru must not be eaten if it lacks purification. / For all the evil of a human being resides in food.
Whoever eats another's food eats his sin. / A sharecropper, a family friend, a cowherd, and a barber—
among Śūdras, their food may be eaten; and whoever offers himself [into service], / an actor, an artisan, and a field-worker—
these are Śūdras whose food may be eaten, having seen their few faults, by the wise. / Milk-rice, food cooked in fat or oil, cow's milk products, and roasted barley meal,
oil-cake, and oil may indeed be accepted from a Śūdra by the twice-born. / Eggplant, *nālikā* greens, safflower, and ash-pumpkin;
onion, garlic, sour fermented gruel, and plant resin should be avoided; / mushrooms, domesticated pork, boiled colostrum,
curdled milk, displeasing food, and plant-shoots should be avoided; / carrots, *kiṃśuka*, and pumpkin;
eating *udumbara* and bottle-gourd, a twice-born indeed falls. / Likewise, *kṛsara* dish, *saṃyāva* sweetmeat, milk-rice, and fried cake;
meat that has not been offered in ritual, food dedicated to deities, sacrificial oblations, / barley gruel, citron, and fish that have not been offered in ritual;
the *nīpa*, wood-apple, and *plakṣa* fig should be avoided with effort; / oil-cake from which oil has been extracted, and wild grain dedicated to gods;
at night, anything associated with sesame, and curd should be abandoned with effort; / one must not eat buttermilk with milk, nor make use of inedibles.
Food spoiled by worms, tainted in disposition, and in contact with earth should be avoided, / as well as food fallen upon by worms or insects, and food continuously moistened by friends[' weeping];
food smelled by a dog, cooked a second time, looked upon by a Caṇḍāla, / [touched] by a menstruating woman, by outcasts, or smelled by cows;
food served irregularly, stale food, and food overturned; / food touched by a crow or cock, and infested with worms;
smelled by human beings, or touched by a leper; / given by a menstruating woman, a harlot, or a diseased woman;
or [given by one] wearing filthy garments, or one wearing another's clothes—one should avoid it. / The milk of a cow whose calf has died, and of a sheep before ten days [from birthing],
sheep's milk, and the milk of a cow in heat are undrinkable, so Manu declared. / The crane, swan, water-hen, sparrow, parrot,
osprey, pheasant, web-footed bird, cuckoo, / crows, wagtails, hawk, and vulture;
owl, ruddy shelduck, falcon, dove, / pigeon, lapwing, and village fowl;
lion, tiger, cat, dog, pig, / jackal, monkey, and donkey—one must not eat [these].
One must not eat snakes, wild beasts, peafowl, and other forest-dwellers, / water-dwellers, or land-dwellers—this is the established rule.
The monitor lizard, tortoise, hare, rhinoceros, and porcupine, O best of men: / Manu, lord of creatures, declared these five-nailed creatures to be always edible.
One may eat fish with scales, and the flesh of the *ruru* deer, / having offered it first to the deities and to the brāhmaṇas, but not otherwise.
Peacock, francolin, dove, and francolin partridge, / the *vārdhrīṇasa* crane, [specific] fish, and the swan that has been overpowered,
the *śapharī*, the lion-head fish, and likewise the *pāṭhīna* and *rohita* fish— / these fish are declared edible, O best of the twice-born.
One may eat their consecrated meat at the desire of a brāhmaṇa, / or when employed according to rule, or at the peril of one's life.

One should not otherwise eat meats; one eating the sacrificial remnants is not tainted, / or [when eaten] for medicinal purposes, or when one is incapable, or by injunction, or for the sake of sacrifice.
And he who, having been invited to an ancestral rite or a rite to the gods, rejects meat, / goes to hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal.
Not to be given, not to be drunk, or not to be touched, / and never even to be looked upon by the twice-born—such is the rule regarding liquor.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always avoid liquor. / Having drunk it, a twice-born falls from his duties and becomes unfit to be spoken to.
Even having eaten inedibles or drunk undrinkables, a twice-born / does not become eligible [for rites] until he passes it downwards.
Therefore, a wise man should always avoid inedibles with effort, / as well as undrinkables; if he does otherwise, he goes to Raurava.

3.57.m: Vyāsa said: / Now therefore I shall expound the unsurpassed duty of giving, / spoken formerly by Brahmā to the sages who expound the Veda.
The fitting presentation of wealth to a worthy recipient with faith / is defined as a gift, bestowing the fruit of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever gives to distinguished persons, endowed with the highest faith, / that indeed I consider truly given; the rest merely protects someone's [possession].
Regular, occasional, and desired—giving is declared to be threefold; / a fourth is called pure, the highest of all gifts.
Whatever is given day after day to one who has done no favor, / without intending any fruit from it, to a brāhmaṇa, is the regular [gift].
Whatever is given into the hand of the wise for the pacification of sin, / that occasional gift is declared by the virtuous to be unsurpassed.
Whatever is given for offspring, victory, sovereignty, and happiness, / that gift is termed desired by the sages who contemplate dharma.
Whatever is given to knowers of the Veda for the pleasure of the Lord, / with a mind united with dharma, that gift is pure and auspicious.
One should practice the duty of giving according to one's capacity, having found a worthy recipient; / for that recipient is approached who delivers [one] from everything.
What remains over after the feeding and clothing of the family should be given; / if it is given otherwise, that gift does not bear fruit.
To a learned scholar of the Veda, of noble family, humble, ascetic, / observing vows, and impoverished, it should be given with devotion.
Whoever gives land with devotion to a brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fire / goes to the supreme abode, having gone where he does not grieve.
A land endowed with sugarcane, possessing barley and wheat, / he who gives [it] to a knower of the Veda is not born again.
Even a piece of land measuring only a cow's hide, / whoever gives [it] to a poor brāhmaṇa is freed from all sins.
No gift is found in this world superior to the gift of land; / the gift of food is equal to it, and the gift of knowledge is greater than that.
Whoever gives knowledge according to rule to a tranquil, / pure brāhmaṇa who is devoted to dharma, is honored in the world of Brahmā.
One should give gold daily with faith to a religious student; / freed from all sins, he attains the abode of Brahmā.
By giving food to a householder, a man obtains fruit; / food alone should be given to him; having given it, he attains the supreme state.
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, [one should feed] five or seven brāhmaṇas, / having fasted according to rule, tranquil, pure, with concentrated mind,
having worshiped especially with black sesame seeds and honey, / when in his mind there is the thought: 'May Dharmarāja be pleased!'
Whatever sin has been committed throughout life is destroyed at that very instant. / Having placed sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter on a black antelope skin,
Whoever gives [this] to a brāhmaṇa overcomes all misdeeds, / especially rice with clarified butter and a water-pot on the full moon of Vaiśākha.
Offering [it] to Dharmarāja and giving it to brāhmaṇas, he is freed from fear; / or if with [pots] accompanied by gold and sesame seeds he gratifies seven or five brāhmaṇas
with vessels of water, he wipes away [even] the murder of a brāhmaṇa. / In the month of Māgha, during the dark fortnight, having fasted on the twelfth [day],
wearing white garments, having sacrificed into the fire with black sesame seeds, / collected in mind, he should give those very sesame seeds to brāhmaṇas.
Whatever sin has been committed since birth, the twice-born indeed overcomes it all. / Coming to the new moon day, to an ascetic brāhmaṇa,
whatever he may give dedicated to Keśava, the lord of the god of gods, [saying,] / ‘May Lord Viṣṇu, eternal Hṛṣīkeśa, be pleased!’—
the sin committed across seven births is destroyed that very moment. / But he who, having bathed on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, should worship
the trident-bearing god Pinākin through the mouth of a twice-born, has no rebirth. / Especially on the eighth of the dark fortnight, to a righteous twice-born,
having bathed and worshipped according to rule with the washing of the feet and the like, / [saying,] ‘May Mahādeva be pleased with me,’ he should give his own wealth.
Freed from all sins, he attains the supreme state. / Especially on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight and on the eighth of the dark fortnight, by twice-borns,
and on the new moon day, Trivikrama is to be worshipped by the devoted. / Fasting on the eleventh day, on the twelfth day
he should worship Puruṣottama through the mouth of a brāhmaṇa; he goes to the supreme abode. / This tithi of the bright fortnight, the twelfth, is sacred to Viṣṇu;
on it he should diligently worship the god Janārdana. / Whatever is given dedicated to the god, the Supreme Lord, to a pure brāhmaṇa,
or even to Viṣṇu, that is remembered as bearing endless fruit. / For whichever deity a man desires to worship fully,
he should diligently honour brāhmaṇas, and from that he pleases that [deity]. / Residing in the bodies of the twice-born, the deities constantly remain;
when a brāhmaṇa cannot be found, they are worshipped in images and the like somewhere. / Therefore, desiring the fruit with effort in images and the like,
the deity is always to be worshipped especially in twice-borns. / One who desires glory should constantly worship Puraṃdara;
one who desires brahmic splendor should worship Brahmā; one who desires knowledge, [the same]; / one who desires health, the Sun; one who desires wealth, Fire;
one who desires the success of actions should indeed worship Vināyaka; / one who desires enjoyments, the Moon; one who desires strength, the Wind;
the seeker of liberation from all saṃsāra should diligently worship Hari. / But he who seeks yoga as well as liberation and sovereign knowledge
should diligently worship the three-eyed Virūpākṣa, lord of the gods. / Those who desire great enjoyments and knowledge [worship] Maheśvara;
those pleasure-seekers worship the lord of beings and Keśava as well. / A giver of water attains satisfaction, and the gift of water is greater than that.
A giver of oil gains desired offspring; a giver of lamps, excellent sight; / a giver of land obtains everything; a giver of gold, long life;
a giver of a house, foremost mansions; a giver of silver, excellent beauty; / a giver of clothes, dwelling in the realm of the Moon; a giver of a horse, an excellent vehicle;
a giver of food, his desired prosperity; a giver of a cow, the world of the brāhmaṇas; / a giver of vehicles and beds, a wife; a giver of fearlessness, sovereignty;
a giver of grain, perpetual happiness; a giver of the Veda, the eternal Brahman. / One should also bestow grain according to one’s capacity upon twice-borns
distinguished by Vedic learning; dying, he enjoys heaven. / And by the donation of cattle and food, he is freed from all sins;
by the gift of firewood, a man is born with a bright [digestive] fire. / Fruits, roots, drinks, and various vegetables
he should give to brāhmaṇas, and he will always be filled with joy. / Medicine, oil, and food for a sick person to alleviate illness—
he who gives [these] is free from disease, happy, and long-lived indeed. / The path of the Sword-Leaved Forest, beset with razor-sharp edges
and intense heat, is crossed by the man who gives an umbrella and sandals. / Whatever is most cherished in the world and whatever is desired in one's home,
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one desiring it to become imperishable. / At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during eclipses of the moon and sun,
and at times such as the solar transits, what is given becomes imperishable. / Having given at pilgrimage places like Prayāga, at sacred temples,
and at river springs, he attains the imperishable. / There is no dharma for living beings in this world higher than the duty of giving.
Therefore, gifts should be given to a brāhmaṇa, a master of the Veda, by twice-borns, / for heaven, by one desiring prosperity, and likewise for the appeasement of sin.
And by a seeker of liberation, gifts should be given daily to brāhmaṇas. / But that unrighteous person who out of delusion obstructs that which is being given
to cows, brāhmaṇas, fire, and the gods goes to an animal womb. / But he who, having acquired wealth, does not worship brāhmaṇas and gods,
the king, having confiscated his entire property, should banish him from the realm. / He who, in a time of famine, does not give food and the like
while brāhmaṇas are dying, that brāhmaṇa is truly despised. / They should not accept [gifts] from him, nor should they dwell with him;
Having learned [of him], the king should banish him from his kingdom; / afterwards he gives his own wealth, the means of righteousness, to good people here.
that sinner, worse than before, is cooked in hell. / To those brāhmaṇas who are devoted to Vedic recitation, learned, with senses subdued,
endowed with truth and restraint—to them, O best of twice-borns, one should give. / One should feed a learned, righteous twice-born even if he has already eaten,
and not a fool devoid of good conduct, even if he has fasted for ten nights. / He who bypasses a learned brāhmaṇa who is nearby and gives [to another],
that sinner by that deed burns his family up to the seventh generation. / If a twice-born should himself be superior in good conduct, learning, and the like,
to him it should diligently be given, even bypassing proximity. / He who receives with reverence and gives with reverence,
both of them go to heaven, but in the opposite case, to hell. / One should not give even water to a nihilist or to a rationalist,
nor to any heretics, nor to one ignorant of the Veda, [so knows] one who knows dharma. / If an unlearned man should accept silver, gold,
a cow, a horse, land, or sesame seeds, he turns to ashes like wood. / The best of the twice-born should seek wealth from praiseworthy twice-borns,
even from a kṣatriya or a vaiśya, but under no circumstances from a śūdra. / He should seek restriction of livelihood; he should not desire accumulation of wealth.
For one intent on the greed for wealth falls away from the very status of a brāhmaṇa. / Having studied all the Vedas and having performed sacrifices in every way,
he does not attain that state which he might attain from contentment. / He should have no taste for accepting gifts, and he should not collect from a śūdra;
taking more than is necessary for subsistence, a brāhmaṇa goes to a low destination. / But he who does not attain contentment is not a vessel for heaven;
he torments living beings just as a thief does. / Desiring to maintain a spiritual teacher and servants, and gratifying deities and guests,
he may accept from all, but he himself should not be satisfied from that. / Thus the householder, steadfast in self, worshipping deities and guests,
living with controlled self, goes to that supreme abode. / Having entrusted his wife to his sons and gone to the forest, the knower of reality,

He should wander constantly alone, detached and concentrated. / This dharma of householders has been declared to you, best of the twice-born; / knowing it, one should strictly abide [by it] and likewise cause the twice-born to perform it.

One who thus perpetually worships the Lord, the one beginningless God, through the duty of a householder, / passes beyond the womb of all beings, attains the supreme Prakṛti, and takes no further birth.

3.58.m: Vyāsa said: / Having thus dwelt in the householder stage for the second part of life, / one should enter the forest-dweller stage, along with one's wife and sacred fire,
or, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go to the forest, / upon seeing the offspring of his offspring and with his body worn by age.
In the forenoon of the bright fortnight, during the auspicious northern course of the sun, / having gone to the forest, restrained by vows, he should practice asceticism with concentrated mind.
He should always gather pure fruits and roots as food; / with whatever food he eats, he should worship the ancestors and the deities.
He should always honor guests, and after bathing, worship the gods; / having obtained eight morsels [of food] from a house, he should eat them with concentrated mind.
He should always wear matted hair, and should not discard his nails or body hair; / he should perform sacred study in every manner, and restrain his speech from all else.
He should offer the Agnihotra and perform the five great sacrifices, / with various pure wild vegetables, roots, or fruits that have grown.
He should always be dressed in bark garments, bathe three times a day, pure, / showing compassion to all beings and refraining from receiving gifts.
The twice-born should regularly sacrifice on the new moon and full moon, / and he should perform seasonal sacrifices, first-fruits offerings, and four-month observances,
and in succession the northern and southern courses of the sun, / with pure spring and autumn wild products collected by himself.
He should properly offer cakes and boiled grains separately according to rule; / having offered exceedingly pure oblation to the gods and ancestors,
he should eat the remainder, along with salt made by himself. / He should avoid intoxicating drink, meat, and earthly mushrooms,
bhūstṛṇa grass, young sprout-grass, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree; / he should not eat what is grown on plowed land, even if abandoned by someone,
nor village-grown flowers and fruits, even when distressed. / According to the Śrāvaṇa rule alone, he should always tend the fire.
He should not bear malice toward any living beings; he should be free of dualities and fearless; / he should eat nothing at night, and at night he should be devoted to meditation.
With senses conquered and anger subdued, reflecting on the knowledge of truth, / he should always remain celibate, not even resorting to his wife.
If one goes to the forest with his wife and engages in sexual intercourse out of desire, / his vow is broken, and that twice-born must undergo expiation.
The child who is born there must not be touched by the twice-born; / nor indeed does he have any right to the Veda, and likewise in his lineage as well.
He should constantly sleep on the ground, devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī, / a refuge for all beings, always intent upon sharing with the good.
He should avoid speaking ill of others, false speech, sleep, and laziness; / he should maintain a single fire, be without a dwelling, and resort to sprinkled ground.
Subdued, he should roam with the deer and live among them; / he should sleep on a rock or on gravel, fully concentrated.
He may be one who consumes for the day, or one who stores for a month, / or one who stores for six months, or one who stores for a year.
He should eat food at night, having gathered it by day according to his ability; / or he may eat at the fourth meal-time, or even at the eighth meal-time.
Or by the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow he should diminish food in the bright and dark fortnights; / every half-month he should eat boiled barley gruel once.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits / that are natural and fallen of themselves, adhering to the Vaikhānasa doctrine.
Or he may roll on the ground, or stand on tiptoe all day; / he should spend time in standing and sitting, and never abandon fortitude.
In summer he should endure the five fires; in the rainy season he should stay under the open sky; / and in winter he should wear wet clothes, gradually increasing his ascetic heat.
He should bathe three times a day and gratify the ancestors and the gods; / he should stand on one foot, or constantly drink in the sun's rays.
He may be one who inhales the smoke of the five fires, one who absorbs heat, or a drinker of soma; / he should drink milk in the bright fortnight and cow dung in the dark fortnight.
He may feed on fallen leaves, or continually subsist by difficult penances; / he should be devoted to the practice of yoga and always recite the Rudrādhyāya,
a reciter of the Atharvaśiras, dedicated to the study of Vedānta; / unwearied, he should always observe the restraints and observances.
Then, having deposited the fires within himself, intent upon meditation,
fireless, without a dwelling, the sage should be intent upon liberation; / he should collect alms just for sustenance among ascetic brāhmaṇas,
and among other twice-born householders who dwell in the forest; / or living in the forest, he may gather eight morsels from a village and eat them,
receiving them in a leaf-cup, in his bare hand, or in an earthenware fragment; / and he should mutter various Upaniṣads for the attainment of the Self,

as well as special lores, the Sāvitrī, and likewise the Rudrādhyāya; / or established in the rite of offering himself to Brahman, he may undertake the great departure, fasting to death, / entering the fire, or other [means].

3.59.m: Vyāsa said: / Having thus dwelt in the forest hermitage for the third part of life, / one should sequentially spend the fourth part of life in renunciation.
Having established the fires within himself, the twice-born should become a mendicant, / devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, intent upon the knowledge of Brahman.
When dispassion toward all objects has arisen in his mind, / then he should desire renunciation; in the opposite case, he would fall.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or else the Āgneyī, / self-controlled, dressed in white or reddish-brown cloth, he should resort to the stage of Brahman.
Some are renunciants through knowledge; others are renunciants through the Veda; / yet others are renunciants through action: they are declared to be of three kinds.
He who is completely liberated from everything, free from dualities, and fearless, / established in the Self alone, is called a renunciant through knowledge.
He who constantly studies the Veda alone, free from desire and without possessions, / seeking liberation, with subdued senses, is called a renunciant through the Veda.
The twice-born who, having internalized the sacred fire, is dedicated to offering everything to Brahman, / devoted to the great sacrifices, is to be known as a renunciant through action.
Among these three, the one endowed with knowledge is considered superior; / for that wise man there is no duty, nor any emblem of an ascetic.
Free from mineness, fearless, tranquil, free from dualities, subsisting on leaves, / he should wear a worn loincloth, or go naked, intent upon meditation.
Celibate, restrained in diet, he should gather food from a village; / delighting in the inner Self, he should remain indifferent and without expectations.
With only himself as his companion, he should wander here for the sake of bliss; / he should not welcome death, nor should he welcome life;
he should just await the time, as a servant awaits his order; / he should not study, nor engage in occupation, nor ever listen [to worldly talk].
Thus the yogin devoted to knowledge is fit for becoming Brahman, / whether the wise man wears a single garment or merely a loincloth.
He may be shaven-headed or have a topknot, or carry a triple staff, devoid of possessions, / wearing ochre robes, constantly devoted to meditation and yoga.
He should dwell at the edge of a village, at the root of a tree, or in a temple, / equal toward an enemy as toward a friend, and likewise in honor and dishonor.
He should always subsist on alms and never eat food from a single household; / but a renouncer who, through delusion or otherwise, eats food from a single household,
for him no expiation whatsoever is seen in the law-books. / His inner self free from passion and aversion, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
refraining from injury to living beings, he should keep silence, free from all desires. / He should set down his foot purified by sight; he should drink water purified by cloth.
He should speak speech purified by truth; he should act with a mind purified. / Except during the rainy season, the mendicant should not dwell in one single place.
Having bathed, always endowed with purity, holding a water-pot in hand, clean, / always delighting in celibacy, he should delight in forest-dwelling.
Devoted to the treatises on liberation, wearing the sacred thread, with conquered senses, / freed from hypocrisy and egoism, devoid of censure and slander,
endowed with the virtue of self-knowledge, if he would attain liberation, / he should constantly practice the eternal deity named Praṇava.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, pure in temples and like places, / wearing the sacred thread, calm in mind, with kuśa grass in hand, concentrated,
dressed in washed ochre garments, his body hair covered by them, / he should mutter the Brahman related to the sacrifice and that related to the deities,
and constantly that related to the self, which is declared in the Upaniṣads. / Or, residing among sons, a celibate student, an ascetic, a silent sage,
he should constantly recite only the Veda; he goes to the supreme state. / Non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, supreme austerity,
forbearance, compassion, and contentment are especially his vows. / Or, intent on the knowledge of the Upaniṣads, concentrated, the five sacrifices
he should perform day after day, having bathed; only for the purpose of alms, indeed, / he should constantly mutter the homa mantras at the proper times, concentrated.
And he should perform his daily Vedic recitation every day, and mutter the Sāvitrī at the two twilights; / he should constantly meditate on the solitary deity, the supreme Lord.

He should always avoid food from a single house, lust, anger, and possessions. / Wearing one garment or two garments, having a topknot, possessing a sacred thread, / a wise man with a water-pot in hand, carrying a triple staff, an ascetic goes beyond that.

3.60.m: Vyāsa said: / Thus subsistence for self-controlled ascetics steadfast in their stage of life / has been declared to be by means of alms, or else by fruits and roots.
He should go for alms at a single time [a day], and he should not attach himself to abundance; / for an ascetic attached to alms becomes attached to sensory objects as well.
He should wander to seven houses for alms; if he obtains nothing, he may wander again. / The mendicant should stand with face cast down only for the time it takes to milk a cow.
Having said "alms" just once, restrained in speech and pure, he should silently receive it. / Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water according to the rule,
having shown the food to the sun, a man should eat facing east. / Having offered the five vital-breath offerings, he should eat eight mouthfuls, collected in mind.
Having sipped water, he should meditate on the deity, the Brahman, the supreme Lord. / A bottle-gourd, a wooden vessel, an earthen pot, and also one made of bamboo—
Manu, the lord of creatures, declared these four as the vessels of an ascetic. / In the early part of the night, in the middle of the night, and likewise in the later part of the night,
he should constantly contemplate the Lord, especially at the twilight recitations. / Having established within the lotus of the heart the one named All, the source of all,
the Self of all beings, standing beyond darkness, / the support of everything, unmanifest, bliss, imperishable light,
transcending primordial matter and the spirit, the space, the fire, auspicious, / the ultimate end of all states of existence, the Lord whose form is Brahman;
or having resolved the self into the supreme Self at the end of the sound Oṃ, / he should meditate on the divine Īśāna in space, situated within space,
the cause of all states of existence, the sole resting-place of bliss; / meditating upon the ancient spirit, Viṣṇu, he is released from bondage.
Or having contemplated in the primal cave, in nature, the abode of cosmic delusion, / the supreme space, the sole cause of all beings,
the life of all beings, in which the world dissolves, / the subtle bliss of Brahman which seekers of liberation behold—
having contemplated Brahman placed in its midst, pure, characterized by knowledge, / infinite, truth, Īśāna, he should remain restrained in speech.
This has been declared as the most secret knowledge of secrets for ascetics. / One who ever abides by this attains sovereign yoga.
Therefore, always delighting in knowledge, devoted to the science of the Self, / he should diligently practice the knowledge that is Brahman, by which he is released from bondage.
Knowing the Self as distinct and pure from everything else, / bliss, imperishable knowledge, he should then meditate on that supreme [reality],
from which beings arise and having known which one is not born here again; / that divine Lord is beyond that, he who presides over it,
within whom is that movement, eternal, auspicious, imperishable; / he who is beyond this self, he indeed is the god Maheśvara.
Whatever vows belong to mendicants, and likewise these vows [prescribed], / by the violation of each one an expiation is enjoined.
Having approached a woman out of lust, he should, composed and pure, / perform the sāṃtapana penance accompanied by breath-control.
Then, with his mind restrained, he should observe a penance according to rule; / returning to his hermitage, the mendicant should live unwearied.
The wise hold that an untruth connected with dharma does not injure; / nevertheless, such association, being terrible, must not be made.
A fast for one night and a hundred breath-controls / must be performed by an ascetic desiring dharma after speaking an untruth.
Even when fallen into extreme distress, theft must never be committed from another; / there is no unrighteousness greater than theft: so stands the tradition.
Violence, excessive craving, and begging destroy knowledge of the self; / this which is called wealth is truly the external vital breaths.
Whoever takes away someone's wealth takes away his vital breaths. / Having acted thus, that wicked-minded man, broken in conduct, fallen from his vows,
having again attained world-weariness, the mendicant should live untiringly. / But if a mendicant should commit an act of injury unexpectedly,
If through weakness of the senses an ascetic discharges [semen] upon seeing a woman, / he should perform a kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or a cāndrāyaṇa penance.
sixteen breath-controls must indeed be held by him. / If he emits semen by day, the wise say there should be a three-night [fast] and a hundred breath-controls.
In the case of eating food from a single house, honey, meat, and likewise at a new ancestral offering, / and in the case of visible salt, the prājāpatya penance is prescribed as the purification.
All sin of one who is constantly intent on meditation is destroyed; / therefore, having meditated on Nārāyaṇa, he should be intent on meditation upon him.
The supreme light of Brahman, entered into the imperishable and undecaying, / that inner Self which is the supreme Brahman—that is to be known as Maheśvara.
This god is Mahādeva, pure, the supreme Śiva; / that alone is the imperishable, non-dual; that is the eternal supreme state.
Therefore he is exalted in the deity, in his own abode termed knowledge; / from the union of the self with the supreme principle, he is thus called Mahādeva.
He who perceives no other god distinct from Mahādeva, / and pursues that very Self, goes to the supreme state.
Those who consider their own self to be separate from the Supreme Lord / do not see that God; their exertion is in vain.
The single supreme Brahman alone should be known as the imperishable reality; / that God is indeed Mahādeva—having known this, one is not bound.
Therefore, the ascetic, with restrained mind, should strive constantly: / delighting in the yoga of knowledge, peaceful, devoted solely to Mahādeva.
This auspicious stage of life of ascetics has been told to you, O brāhmaṇas, / which was formerly spoken by the grandfather, the all-pervading sage.
One should never give this unexcelled, auspicious knowledge, / which rests on the duties of ascetics and was proclaimed by the Self-born, to anyone other than a son, a disciple, or a yogin.

Thus has been spoken this rule of the ascetics' observances, which is the sole cause for the pleasure of the best of gods. / There is no rebirth or destruction again for those who, with well-disposed minds, constantly practice it.

3.61.m: Sūta said: / When the brāhmaṇas had been thus addressed long ago by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, / the venerable Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, having spoken this much,
Having consoled all the sages, he went away just as he had come. / "The rule of castes and stages of life has indeed been told to you by me.
having acted thus, one becomes dear to Viṣṇu, never otherwise. / I will tell you the secret regarding that; listen, O best of the twice-born.
The duties based on castes and stages of life that were taught here, O twice-born, / are not equal even to a tiny fraction of devotion to Hari.
Devotion to Hari alone is indeed to be accomplished by men in the Kali age; / in another age, duties are indeed to be practiced by man.
In the Kali [age], he who worships the god Nārāyaṇa possesses dharma; / having placed in his heart Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, the much-invoked, eternal,
supreme, and tranquil [Lord], the three worlds are surely conquered by him. / From the bite of the serpent of the time of Kali, from sin, and from the Kālakūṭa poison,
a twice-born, having drunk the nectar of devotion to Hari, transcends [all danger]. / What is the use of recitations if the name of Śrī Hari has been taken by men?
What is the use of ablutions for one who carries the water from Viṣṇu's feet on his head? / What is the use of a sacrifice for one who has held the lotus feet of Hari in his heart?
What is the use of charity if the deed of Hari is proclaimed in the assembly? / He who rejoices again and again upon hearing the hosts of Hari's virtues—
that state belongs to one whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa, rejoicing through meditation. / Those skilled in the speech of heretics are said to be obstacle-makers there;
women and those attached to them are also destroyers of devotion to Hari. / The command of women's glances is hard to conquer even for the gods;
he by whom it is conquered in the world is called a devotee of Hari. / Even sages become intoxicated here, covetous of women's behavior.

Whence can devotion to Hari arise for men devoted to women, O twice-born? / Female demons disguise themselves as desirable women and roam the world, O twice-born; / they constantly make a morsel of men's intellect.
Only so long does learning prevail, only so long does knowledge operate, / only so long is the intellect perfectly clear, retaining all the scriptures,
only so long is there recitation, so long austerity, so long resort to sacred fords, / only so long service to the guru, only so long an inclination toward giving,
only so long is there awakening, only so long indeed is there discernment, / only so long a relish for the company of the good, only so long a desire for the Purāṇas,
so long as the rolling of a woman's restless eyes does not fall upon a person, / [causing] the destruction of all dharma, O brāhmaṇas.
In that matter, those who are graced by a drop of honey from the lotus feet of Hari— / the casting of women's restless eyes cannot overpower them.
Those by whom service to Hṛṣīkeśa has been performed birth after birth, O twice-born, / who have given to twice-borns and sacrificed into the fire, have dispassion in this and that.
What indeed is called the beauty of women? / It is said to be the glitter of ornaments and clothes.
Devoid of love and self-knowledge, whence is a woman's form glorified? / Full of pus, urine, feces, blood, skin, fat, bone, and marrow—
that is called a body; whence is there beauty in this? / Having thus reflected upon it separately, one should bathe after touching it and become pure.
Composed of these, a body is indeed seen as beautiful by people. / Ah, the misfortune of men brought about by ill fate, O twice-born!
A man pursues a body covered with breasts, thinking it to be a woman. / Who is a woman, or who is a man, when there is any true reflection?
Therefore, a good man should avoid association with women with all his soul. / Who indeed, having resorted to a woman, attains spiritual perfection on earth?
One should completely abandon an alluring woman and company with those who associate with alluring women. / From association with them comes [the hell] Raurava—this is directly perceived.
Out of ignorance, people are covetous, deceived there by fate. / A man cooks in this direct hell-pit: a woman's womb.
From where he came into the world, in that very thing he delights again; / from which urine, semen, and filthy waste constantly flow,
in that very place a person delights! Who could be more impure than he? / In this world, that is the greatest suffering; ah, the mockery of fate!
Again and again he delights there—ah, the shamelessness of men! / Therefore, a wise man should reflect upon the numerous faults of women.
From sexual intercourse, loss of strength occurs; sleep becomes overly vigorous; / robbed of knowledge by sleep, a man becomes short-lived.
Therefore, the wise man should zealously view a woman like his own death; / an intelligent person should delight his mind in the lotus feet of Govinda.
For serving Govinda's feet brings happiness in this world and the next; / having abandoned that, what great fool serves a woman's feet?
For service to the feet of Janārdana bestows non-return [to rebirth], / but service to women's vulva causes distress in the womb.
Again and again he falls into the womb, like [sugarcane] crushed in a press; / again he desires that very thing; one should know this to be a mockery of thieves.
With uplifted arms I proclaim—listen to my supreme word: / Fix your heart on Govinda, not on the vulva which partakes of torment!
And the man who conducts himself having completely abandoned the company of women / obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
If by stroke of fate a chaste woman of good family is married by men, / he who, having begotten a son with her, then completely avoids association with her,
with him the Lord of the World becomes pleased, there is no doubt. / For association with women is declared by knowers of dharma to be bad company;
while it exists, very firm devotion to Hari does not arise at all. / Having abandoned all attachment, one should practice devotion to Hari.
And devotion to Hari in this world is considered by me to be rare indeed; / he who has devotion to Hari has attained his goal, there is no doubt.
One should perform that very action by which Hari is pleased; / when he is pleased, the world is pleased; when he is satisfied, the world is satisfied.
Without devotion to Hari, the birth of men is declared to be in vain; / he for whose pleasure gods such as Brahmā and Īśa sacrifice—
what person would not serve that unmanifest Nārāyaṇa? / Highly fortunate is his mother, of great merit is his father,
By him whose heart holds the pair of Janārdana's feet, / O Janārdana, worshipful to the universe, affectionate to those who come for refuge!"
those mortals who utter this have no path to hell. / Brāhmaṇas especially are visibly the embodiments of Hari.
If they worship [them] properly, Hari is pleased with them. / Viṣṇu wanders this earth in the form of a brāhmaṇa.
Without a brāhmaṇa, no ritual action attains success at all. / By those who with devotion have drunk the water from a twice-born's feet and placed it on their head,
the ancestors are satisfied and one's very self is surely delivered. / By whoever sweet, consecrated [food] is placed in the mouth of brāhmaṇas,
it is placed directly in the mouth of Kṛṣṇa; Hari himself surely consumes that. / Ah, people are so very rare when Keśava is visibly present in a twice-born [man]!
They serve [him] in images and the like; that ritual is indeed for his absence. / Because of the presence of brāhmaṇas, the earth is praised as fortunate.
Whatever is placed in their hand is placed in the hand of Hari. / From bowing down to them comes indeed the banishing of sins.
From saluting a vipra, one is freed from sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa. / Therefore, the brāhmaṇa is to be worshipped by the virtuous with the mindset that he is Viṣṇu.
If anything whatsoever is given into the mouth of a hungry twice-born, / after death, streams of nectar sprinkle [the giver] for ten million aeons.
The mouth of a twice-born is a great field, free from barren soil, free from thorns; / if anything is sown therein, one obtains a ten-million-fold fruit.
Having given him a meal with clarified butter, one rejoices for an aeon. / Whoever gives various delicious foods for the pleasure of a twice-born,
his worlds grant great enjoyments and bestow liberation up to ten million aeons. / Placing a brāhmaṇa first, one should constantly listen to the Purāṇa
recited by a brāhmaṇa, [which is] a forest fire for great sins. / Among all sacred places, the Purāṇa is spoken of as the supreme sacred place,
from hearing a single verse-quarter of which Hari himself is pleased. / Just as Hari, having assumed the form of the sun, wanders for the sake of illumination
of all the worlds, Hari [acting] as the cause of light, / even so Hari, whose body is the Purāṇa, for inner illumination
wanders among beings here: the Purāṇa is the supreme purifier. / Therefore, if one's mind is set upon generating love for Hari,
the Purāṇa, which has the form of Kṛṣṇa, should be heard unceasingly by men. / It should be heard, though difficult to obtain, by a peaceful devotee of Viṣṇu,
the pure recitation of the Purāṇa, which is the supreme purifier. / Since, collecting the meaning of the Veda, Hari in the form of Vyāsa
composed the Purāṇa, O vipra, therefore it is supreme. / In the Purāṇa dharma is ascertained, and dharma is Keśava himself.
Therefore, when the Purāṇa is celebrated and heard, one becomes Viṣṇu. / A vipra is visibly Hari himself, and the Purāṇa is of the same nature.
Having attained the union of these two, a man becomes Hari himself. / Likewise, by sprinkling with Gaṅgā water, one destroys one's own sin.
Keśava in liquid form delivers the earth from sin. / If a Vaiṣṇava desires the worship of Viṣṇu,
he should perform the pure sprinkling with Gaṅgā water, the supreme purifier. / The goddess Gaṅgā is celebrated on earth as bestowing devotion to Viṣṇu.
For that Gaṅgā, whose nature is Viṣṇu, causes the expansion of the world.
Toward brāhmaṇas, Purāṇas, the Gaṅgā, cows, and the pippala tree, / unmotivated devotion is to be offered by men with the thought of Nārāyaṇa.
These are determined by the knowers of truth to be the visible forms of Viṣṇu; / therefore, they should constantly be worshipped by one desiring devotion to Viṣṇu.
Without devotion to Viṣṇu, human birth is said to be fruitless. / The ocean of the time of Kali, teeming with crocodiles that are sins,
whose whirlpool is immersion in sense-objects, which is exceedingly frothy with incomprehension, / whose sea-monsters are extremely wicked people, which is terrible and fearful,
and difficult to cross, those cross over who are situated in the boat of devotion to Hari. / Therefore, people should make an effort to accomplish devotion to Viṣṇu.
What happiness does a living creature obtain from listening to unprofitable talk? / One is not attached to the recitation of the pastimes of Hari, whose pastimes are wonderful.
Therefore, wondrous stories mingled with various worldly subjects / should be heard by men if their mind clings to sense-objects;
or if the mind is fixed on nirvāṇa, it should still be heard, O twice-born ones! / Even from listening casually, Hari becomes pleased with him.
Though actionless, Hṛṣīkeśa performed various actions / for the sake of the welfare of his devoted hearers, affectionate toward his devotees.
He is not attained by ritual actions, even a hundred Vājapeya [sacrifices], / nor by ten thousand Rājasūya [sacrifices], as he is attained through devotion.
The abode which should be served with the mind, frequented constantly by the good, / the essence in crossing the ocean of worldly existence—take refuge in the abode of Hari!
O! You vulgar, harsh men, greedy for sensual pleasures! / Why indeed will you throw yourselves into the Raurava hell through your own doing?
Without serving Govinda's gentle feet, it will not come to pass; / if you desire an effortless crossing of sorrows,
worship Kṛṣṇa's feet, the cause of non-rebirth! / From where did a mortal come, and to where would he go again?
Having reflected on this, an intelligent person should resort to the accumulation of dharma. / If a person, having arisen from falling into various hells,
having obtained an immovable or other body, through good fortune again / attains human birth, dwelling in the womb there is exceedingly sorrowful.
Then, if by the force of karma the creature is born on earth, / he becomes afflicted by the numerous defects of childhood and so forth, O twice-born.
Again, having reached youth, he is afflicted by poverty, / or by severe illness, and likewise by drought and the like.
In old age he incurs indescribable affliction here and there; / from the unsteadiness of mind, from disease, he then meets with death.
No greater sorrow than that is experienced even in saṃsāra. / Then, by the force of karma, the creature is tortured in the realm of Yama.
Having suffered extreme torment there, he is born yet again. / The creature is born and dies; he dies and is born again.
Such indeed is the condition of one who has not worshipped the feet of Govinda: / effortless death and trouble-free living
do not happen to one who has not worshipped Govinda's feet. / If wealth exists in the home, what fruit is there in hoarding it?
When he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, will wealth follow him? / Therefore, wealth must be honoured by offering to the twice-born; it gives all happiness.
Giving is a stairway to heaven; giving is the destroyer of sins; / devotion and worship to Govinda is the increaser of great merit.
If there is strength in a mortal, he should not expend it in vain: / one should unweariedly perform dance and song in the presence of Hari.
Whatever people possess, that they should offer to Kṛṣṇa; / what is offered to Kṛṣṇa grants well-being, while what is offered to others brings unhappiness.
With both eyes one should gaze upon the image and forms of glorious Hari; / with both ears one should day and night attend to Kṛṣṇa's virtues and names.
With the tongue the water from Hari's feet should be tasted by the wise; / with the nose one should smell the tulasī leaf from Govinda's lotus feet.
With the skin having touched a devotee of Hari, with the mind meditating on his abode, / a creature becomes accomplished: here no doubt should be entertained.
A wise person should indeed be fixed in mind upon him, with his heart directed toward him; / in the end, a person reaches him alone: here no doubt should be entertained.
He who, when meditated upon with the mind, bestows his own abode— / what person would not serve that Nārāyaṇa who is without beginning or end?

With a mind constantly restrained upon Viṣṇu's lotus feet, according to one's ability one should make distributions for his pleasure; / one should place reverent devotion and deep love upon his two feet: he indeed shall surely attain honour in the human world.

3.62.m: Sūta said: / Thus, the majesty which in the world is the cause of deliverance for the world, / of that Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord, who bears diverse forms,
is this single body, the Purāṇa; among them, the Pādma is supremely great. / The Brāhma is the head of Hari; the one called Padma is the heart;
the Vaiṣṇava is the right arm; the Śaiva is the left [arm] of the great Lord; / the Bhāgavata is declared to be the thighs; the Nāradīya is the navel;
and the Mārkaṇḍeya is the right foot; the Āgneya is said to be the left; / the Bhaviṣya is the right knee of great-souled Viṣṇu;
the one called Brahmavaivarta is declared to be the left knee; / the Laiṅga is the right ankle; the Vārāha is the left ankle;
the Skānda Purāṇa is the bodily hairs; his skin is remembered as the Vāmana; / the Kaurma is proclaimed to be the back; the Mātsya is extolled as the fat;
the Gāruḍa is declared to be the marrow; the Brahmāṇḍa is sung as the bone. / In this very way did Viṣṇu, Hari, become composed of the Purāṇas as his limbs.
The heart therein is the Pādma, having heard which one enjoys immortality; / this Padma Purāṇa, however, was the god Hari himself.
By teaching even one chapter of it, one is completely freed from all sins. / There, this first one is the Svarga[khaṇḍa], which gives the fruit of the entire Pādma.
Even those who are great sinners, upon hearing the Svargakhaṇḍa, / are released from sins, just like snakes from worn-out skins.
Even if one of extremely vile conduct, cast out from all righteousness, / whatever fruit he would obtain upon hearing the Ādisvarga—
having heard this Ādisvarga, a man obtains that fruit. / In the month of Māgha, having bathed daily at Prayāga,
as a man is freed from sin, so indeed it happens from hearing [this]. / By him a gift of gold equal to his weight has been given, and the entire earth has been given;
by him the distribution has been made that cleared the debt of the poor; / the thousand names of Hari have been recited repeatedly;
likewise all the Vedas have been studied, and respective rituals have been performed; / and many teachers have been established by bestowing livelihoods upon them;
fearlessness was granted by him to people in fear, O twice-born; / the virtuous, the wise, and the righteous have been honoured;
cool water was given between the signs of Aries and Cancer; / and life has indeed been given up by him for the sake of a brāhmaṇa and a cow;
and other good deeds were performed by that wise person / by whom the first section was heard or recited in the assembly.
Having thoroughly studied the Svargakhaṇḍa, he enjoys various pleasures; / having slept peacefully among the women of the inner apartments, he is awakened
by the ringing sounds of tinkling bells and by sweet words; / he shares half the seat of Indra and lives in Indra's world for a long time.
Then he goes to the abode of the Sun, and from there to the realm of the Moon; / having enjoyed pleasures in the abode of the Seven Sages, he then goes to the Pole Star.
And from there, having attained a radiant body in the world of Brahmā / and attained knowledge right there, he reaches supreme nirvāṇa.
The wise person should dwell with the good; he should perform bathing at sacred sites; / a person should converse only with the good, and listen to the true scripture.
There, the Pādma is the great scripture granting the fruit of all the sacred traditions; / and within it, the Svargakhaṇḍa grants the fruit of great merit.

Worship Govinda, bow to Hari alone, the foremost of gods; you will attain exceedingly pure realms of great delights! / Listen, O people, utter the single matchless name of Hari; if you desire an easy crossing over the waves of desires, obtain the things you wish!

Complete is this initial Svargakhaṇḍa, otherwise called the Ādikhaṇḍa, or the Svargakhaṇḍa. / May there be welfare! May there be prosperity!

4.0.s:
atha śrīpādme mahāpurāṇe cutarthaṃ brahmakhaṇḍaṃ prārabhyate
śrīvedavyāsāya namaḥ
4.0.d:
अथ श्रीपाद्मे महापुराणे चुतर्थं ब्रह्मखण्डं प्रारभ्यते
श्रीवेदव्यासाय नमः
4.0.m: Now begins the fourth, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, in the glorious and great Padma Purāṇa. / Obeisance to glorious Vedavyāsa!

4.1.m: Śaunaka said: / When the Kali [age] has arrived, O Sūta, by what action can the deliverance / of living beings come about? Therefore, tell it before me!
Sūta said: / Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, you are the foremost of virtuous souls, / and you constantly wish the welfare of all people.
About this, the omniscient vipra Vyāsa, worshipped by all, / was formerly asked by Jaimini; hear what he said to him, O Vaiṣṇava!
Having prostrated like a stick before Vyāsa, who had mastered all subjects, / the eminent sage questioned the guru, the son of Satyavatī.
Jaimini said: / By what means can liberation be attained by men in the Kali [age]? Tell me, / since mortals have short lifespans and little merit.
Vyāsa said: / From association with the virtuous, O vipra, comes the hearing of sacred scriptures, O lord; / from that arises devotion to Hari, from that knowledge, and from that the final goal.
On earth, a story concerning Viṣṇu does not appeal to a sinful person; / he, however, should be known as the foremost of sinners, O twice-born.
Hearing the narrative of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a Vaiṣṇava becomes overjoyed; / but he who calls it false should be known as the teacher of sinners.
In whatever place, O vipra, the story of Kṛṣṇa takes place, / Jagannātha never leaves that place and goes away.
The vile man who causes an obstacle at the commencement of Kṛṣṇa's story / has no escape from hell for the duration of a hundred manvantaras.
Those who, having heard a Purāṇa story, revile and mock it, / have hells in their very hands, constantly causing them great misery.
Sin accumulated in previous births is destroyed that very moment / for whoever even makes a desire to hear the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
If a man with devotion actually recites the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, / I do not know what glorious state will be his upon hearing it!
Sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa, premature death, / drinking alcohol, and theft—all of the sinner are destroyed.
Having committed a sin, if a mortal turns away from sin afterward, / his sin will be destroyed like a heap of cotton by fire.
If a book containing the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O vipra, is kept in a house, / the messengers of Yama will not approach that house.
Jaimini said: / Whom do they call Vaiṣṇavas? Tell me, O guru, my desire [is] / now to thoroughly know them and their supreme glorification.
Vyāsa said: / If a man, even a sinner, sprinkles the water from the feet of a Vaiṣṇava upon his head with devotion, O twice-born, / what need has he of bathing at sacred places?
Whoever associates with the virtuous for a moment or half a moment, O twice-born, / his sins, headed by the killing of a brāhmaṇa, are destroyed.
In whichever family even a single Vaiṣṇava is born, / though that family be joined with sins, it surely goes to liberation.
Men who are free from violence, hypocrisy, lust, and anger, / and who have abandoned greed and delusion, are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas, O twice-born.
Those devoted to parents, endowed with compassion, engaged in the welfare of all beings, / free from malice, and truthful in speech are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.
Those who are devoted to brāhmaṇas, indifferent toward other men's wives, / and intent upon the observance of the eleventh day—they are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who sing the names of Hari, wear garlands of tulasī,
and are sprinkled with the water of Hari's feet, are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those on whose ears or head an excellent leaf of tulasī
is ever seen, O twice-born one, are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those free from the company of heretics, devoid of hostility toward brāhmaṇas,
and who water the tulasī plant, are to be known as Vaiṣṇava men.

Those who worship Hari, who honor him with tulasī,
who are devoted to giving a daughter in marriage, and who indeed worship guests,

and who listen to the deeds of Viṣṇu, are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇava men.
And also in whose house a śālagrāma stone is established,

who sweep the abode of Hari, promote offerings to the ancestors,
and are filled with compassion for the wretched—they are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who view another's wealth and a brāhmaṇa's property like poison,
and who eat the food-offering of Hari—they are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇava people.

Those devoted to the Vedas and scriptures, protectors of groves of tulasī,
and intent on the vow of Rādhāṣṭamī, are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Those who offer a lamp with faith before Śrī Kṛṣṇa
and do not slander others, are to be recognized as Vaiṣṇavas.

Sūta said:
When asked by Jaimini, Vyāsa answered him in due order.
This is related by me, O brāhmaṇa, having been heard from the guru on that occasion.

Those best of men who listen to this chapter with faith,
freed from all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

4.2.m:
Sūta said:
Listen, Śaunaka, and I will speak of another ancient duty,
the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini, which destroys the sins of listeners.

Jaimini said:
By what deed, O guru, does even a sinful man
go to the temple of the Lord of the world? Tell me that today, O master!

Vyāsa said:
The man who plasters the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
freed from all sins, though weary, goes to the abode of Hari.

And whoever smears it with water—hear in brief, O Jaimini,
I shall tell the merit of that person in the temple of the Lord of the world.

As many particles of dust as are seen there, O best of the twice-born,
for that many thousands of kalpas he shall dwell in the temple of Viṣṇu.

Formerly, in the age called Dvāpara, there was a thief named Daṇḍaka,
a terror to people, a stealer of brāhmaṇa property, and a slayer of friends,

a speaker of untruth, cruel, devoted to pursuing other men's wives,
an eater of cow's flesh, a drinker of liquor, and an associate of heretics,

a destroyer of the livelihoods of twice-born men, a thief of deposits,
a slayer of those who had sought refuge, and covetous of the charms of courtesans.

Once, O best of the twice-born, that dull-minded man went
to someone's temple of Viṣṇu in order to steal Viṣṇu's property.

Then, having entered the doorway, his feet, which were covered with mud,
were completely wiped off on the low ground of the god's house.

By that very action, the hollowed-out ground indeed became leveled.
Then, with two iron skewers, having opened the door quickly with joy,

he entered the house of Hari, which was adorned with an excellent canopy,
abundant with lamps of gold and jewels, and where deep darkness had been dispelled,

rich with the fragrance of various flowers, crowded with various vessels,
and completely filled with the fragrance of perfumed oil.

Then, lying on a charming couch together with Rādhā,
Acyuta, clad in yellow garments, was seen by that thief.

Bowing to the Lord of Rādhikā, he then became free from sin.
[He thought:] 'Shall I take it, or shall I not take it? What would come of this for me?

I am unable to perform service, since I am a thief at all times.
I have need of wealth.' Thus he resolved to take it.

Having thrown onto the ground the silken cloth of the Lord of Kamalā,
he gathered up the goods, and holding them in his hand, he trembled.

Then, by Viṣṇu, the Lord of Māyā, O Jaimini,
all those items made a tremendous noise and indeed fell down.

Abandoning their sound sleep, crying 'What is this?', running,
many people arrived, and with speed the thief [fled].

Abandoning the wealth, terrified, the thief went a little way;
bitten by a deadly snake, he died, his sins departed.

By order of Yama, his messengers, bearing nooses and clubs in their hands,
fanged and clad in skins, arrived to carry him off.

They bound him with a noose of skin and led him by an impassable path.
Seeing him, Śamana, enraged, inquired of his minister:

Yama said:
'What deed has been done by him—is it sin or indeed merit?
Tell me from its root before me, O wise Citragupta!'

Citragupta said:
'Whatever sins were created by the Creator on the surface of the earth,
they were all committed by this fool; this is the truth that has been spoken by me.

Yet listen, O Lord of the world: he also has good merit.
I consider that all his sins have been eradicated by that, O brother.'

Hearing the word of Yama, Citragupta, fearful,
folded his hands and spoke to his own master, O twice-born one:

Citragupta said:
'This foremost of sinners went to steal the property of Hari.
The mud on his feet was wiped away at the door of Hari, O King.

He indeed bowed to him with his head and spoke, filled with humility.
Yama said: 'My temple has become pure today by the dust of your two feet;

I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled, of this there is no doubt!
Go now, O holy one, to the supreme temple of Hari,

abounding in various enjoyments, which puts an end to birth and death.'
Vyāsa said: Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja, in a chariot made of gold,

a divine chariot yoked with royal swans, placed him, whose sins had departed,
and sent him to the abode of the Discus-Bearer, which bestows all happiness.

Having thus entered Vaikuṇṭha, he stayed there in happiness for a long time.
As for those who plaster the temple of Hari with devotion—

what will become of them, I do not know, O best of the twice-born!
Whoever listens to this with devotion, or reads it with concentrated mind,
the sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed indeed, without a doubt.

4.3.m:
Śaunaka said:
Tell me, Sūta, the glorification of the month of Kārttika before me:
what is the fruit of that vow, or what is the fault of one who does not perform it?

Sūta said:
Once formerly, Jaimini, the best of sages, questioned
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī; the sage began to tell this.

Vyāsa said:
Whoever abandons sesame oil and sexual intercourse during the auspicious month of Kārttika,
freed from the sins committed across many births, goes to the house of Hari.
The man who does not give up fish and sexual intercourse in Kārttika / will surely become a foolish hog in every birth.
If a man worships Janārdana with tulasī leaves in Kārttika, / he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice with every leaf.
Whoever worships Madhusūdana with muni flowers in Kārttika / attains liberation, hard for even the gods to reach, through Hari's grace.
And whatever best of men eats muni-greens in Kārttika, / the sin committed throughout a year is destroyed by that single greens.
A man who eats its fruit in Ūrja, which is dear to Hari, / having first offered it to Hari, O Brahmin, [eradicates] sin born of ten million births.
And whoever offers sweet, delicious [food] mixed with ghee to Hari, / completely freed from all sins, goes to Hari's abode.
Whatever man offers even a single lotus to Hari in Kārttika, / at the end, freed from all sins, he goes to Viṣṇu's realm.
Whatever man takes his morning bath in Kārttika, which is dear to Śrī Hari, / obtains the fruit gained by bathing in all sacred bathing places.
If a twice-born man raises a lamp into the sky in Kārttika, / freed from sins such as killing a Brahmin, he goes to Hari's abode.
O best of Brahmins, even if he raises a lamp into the sky for a single muhūrta in Kārttika for the pleasure of Hari, / Hari is always pleased with him.
