And whatever twice-born offers a lamp with ghee in the house of Kṛṣṇa in Kārttika, / he gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice day after day.
The extraordinary glory of the lamp is declared by me; / listen attentively, O best of Brahmins, to this legendary history.
Formerly, in the Tretā age, there was a pure Brahmin named Vaikuṇṭha, / by the power of whose company even a sinner became liberated.
Once in Kārttika, that Brahmin, a bull among the twice-born, having offered / before Hari a lamp filled with ghee, went home.
A rat arrived at the lamp to taste that ghee; / as he began to eat, that lamp was rekindled [by him].
Out of fear of the fire, the rat quickly fled from there; / and all the rat's sin was destroyed through Hari's grace.
Bitten by a snake, the rat gave up his life. / Then, by order of Yama, messengers holding nooses and clubs in their hands
came to take him away and bound him with leather cords. / Just as they resolved to take him, the messengers of Viṣṇu, bearing conch, discus, and mace,
four-armed and mounted on Garuḍa, arrived. / In the sky was an auspicious celestial chariot accompanied by royal swans,
fashioned of pure gold, moving at will through Hari's grace. / Having cut the noose, those messengers then addressed the attendants of Yama:
“O fools, he is a devotee of Viṣṇu! You have bound him in vain. / Go away, messengers of the Destroyer, if you wish to live!”
Having heard this, trembling and full of humility, they asked: / “By the power of what merit is he being taken by you to [that] city?
He is a great sinner towards Viṣṇu; you should explain that.” / The messengers of Viṣṇu said: “Before Vāsudeva, the rekindling of a lamp was done [by him].
By that very action, O messengers, we are leading him to the abode of Viṣṇu. / Even if one should unintentionally rekindle Viṣṇu's lamp,
abandoning sins accumulated over ten million births, he goes to Hari's abode. / Whoever offers a lamp with devotion during the days of Hari in Kārttika—
no one is able to describe his merit except Hari. / Whoever with devotion offers a lamp filled with ghee in Hari's house,
what need has he for a thousand horse sacrifices? / The performer of a horse sacrifice goes to heaven, [but] on Hari's day,
the giver of a lamp in Kārttika goes to Hari's abode.” / Vyāsa said: Having heard this, those messengers departed just as they had come.
Placing him in the celestial chariot, the messengers of Viṣṇu went to Viṣṇu's abode. / A hundred manvantaras passed for him in the very presence of Viṣṇu.
Then, by the grace of Hari, he became a king's daughter on earth; / endowed with sons and grandsons, she enjoyed pleasures for a long time.
From here she again went to Goloka through service to Hari. / Sūta said: Whatever mortal hears with devotion this excellent glorification of the lamp,
freed from all sins, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.

4.4.m: Śaunaka said: / O Sūta, when is the glorification of Jayantī performed by men? / Tell me, you who are indeed a boat in the ocean of cyclic existence.
Sūta said: / Listen, O Brahmin, best of sages; since I have been asked, I shall proclaim it. / Formerly, Brahmā was asked this by Nārada in the abode of the gods.
Nārada said: / Tell me the glorification of Jayantī, O Grandfather, / hearing which I shall attain that supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: / Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall proclaim it before you. / By fasting on Jayantī, one goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O sage, Jayantī burns away sin accumulated over seven births / through its remembrance and recitation; how much more so for one who fasts?
Janmāṣṭamī, the auspicious bright Navamī in the month of Caitra, / the dark Caturdaśī in Kumbha, the bright Caturdaśī in Meṣa,
Durgāṣṭamī in the bright half of Āśvina, and Dvādaśī combined with Śravaṇā— / six Jayantīs, yielding great merit and conferring auspiciousness, are proclaimed.
The first, Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, is renowned as the destroyer of sins; / it is equal to ten million sacrifices, equal to tens of thousands of sacred bathing places.
The fruit that one who gives a thousand cows day after day obtains, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
[The fruit of giving] a thousand loads of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
[The fruit of giving] thousands of black antelope skins and hundreds of sesame cows, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
Whatever fruit arises from giving ten thousand million virgins [in marriage], / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
Whatever fruit one gains by giving this earth together with the oceans, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
[The fruit of] constructing a reservoir, a well, a pond, and the like at a temple of a deity, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
Whoever is devoted and serves mother, father, and teachers, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
The merit of those whose minds are devoted to the service of sacred bathing places for the removal of misfortune, / and of those who keep vows of truth—[such is the merit] in fasting on Jayantī.
The merit one obtains by bathing in the Gaṅgā, in the Narmadā, / or in the waters of Sarasvatī—[that same] merit he obtains in fasting on Jayantī.
The merit of those performing ancestral rites for the ancestors on the new-moon day, / that same fruit he obtains by fasting on Jayantī.
Nārada said: / Tell me, O Grandfather, by whom was it observed in the past? / Brahmā said: By Kārtavīrya, by Karṇa, and by the wise Kumāra;
it was observed formerly by Sagara, by Dilīpa, and by Kākutstha; / by Gautama, by Gārgya, and by the wise son of Jamadagni;
it was observed formerly by Vālmīki, and by the virtuous son of Draupadī. / The bright eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada bestows desired wishes;
combined with the asterism of Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), that eighth day is especially esteemed. / It should be observed year after year for the pleasure of the Discus-Bearer.
Sin accumulated over ten million births dissolves in a single muhūrta / if, having controlled his senses, he keeps vigil at night with devotion.
He should be worshipped individually with perfumes, flowers, and food-offerings. / Whoever thus observes the Jayantī fast, O brahmin,
his sin accumulated over ten million births, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly,
dissolves within half a watch by the grace of Devakī's son. / Those lowest of men who eat when the Jayantī tithi has arrived,
eat the sin arising from the three worlds, there is no doubt. / All the holy bathing places beginning with the oceans, and all places of liberation,
abide completely in the house of one who observes the Jayantī vow; / all the holy bathing places and the deities abide in his body.
The man who observes with devotion the Jayantī dear to Kṛṣṇa— / neither in the Veda nor in the Purāṇa have I seen anything, O great sage,
equal to that, nor greater, namely, the vow of Kṛṣṇa- and Rādhāṣṭamī. / The man who does not observe it with devotion becomes a cruel rākṣasa.
The foolish man who eats on the day of Jayantī, O twice-born one, / eats great hell, just as on the day of Hari.
One hundred and one generations, both past and future, of his family / certainly fall into a terrifying hell through eating on Jayantī.
And when Jayantī occurs on a Wednesday together with Rohiṇī, / O tiger among sages, what need is there of ten million other vows?
Whether observed in the Kṛta age, the Tretā age, the Dvāpara age, or the Kali age / in accordance with proper procedure, Jayantī destroys sin.
He who causes the Purāṇa to be recited during the vigil for Padmanābha / burns away sin accumulated since birth like a heap of cotton.
The man who hears the Purāṇa with devotion on the day of Hari, / his sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed in that very instant.
One should honor the reciter on the day of Padmanābha, O sage; / having delivered ten million ancestors, he is honored in the realm of Viṣṇu.
The man who turns his face away from fasting on Jayantī / is stripped of all dharma and surely goes to hell.
One should worship with devotional dispositions using perfumes, flowers, incenses, and lamps filled with ghee, / and should give a priestly gift to a brahmin.
The man who observes Jayantī according to this rule, O brahmin, / rescues twenty-one generations of ancestors through devotion.
Neither misfortune nor widowhood, nor discord occurs in his home; / he sees no obstacle to his offspring, nor any loss of wealth.
Whatever desires the one who fasts on Jayantī wishes to attain, / all those he obtains, and he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Those who are ever devoted to Viṣṇu, whose minds are fixed on the Jayantī vow, / they are blessed, they are of noble birth, they are masters, and they are learned.
Whatever holy bathing places, vows, and observances there are, / they are not worth a sixteenth part of the day of Jayantī.
He who, along with his wife, observes the eighth day of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa / in both fortnights of the month of Bhādrapada, dear child, attains the presence of Hari.
He who constantly performs the merit-making vow of Hari, / that faster on Jayantī goes to the Vaikuṇṭha of Viṣṇu.
One devoid of proper conduct, fallen from his family, devoid of fame, or born from an evil womb— / Jayantī, dear to Hari, swiftly destroys his sin.
Sins equal to Mount Meru, such as the killing of a brahmin, / all these the one who fasts on Jayantī burns entirely away.
One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires wealth obtains wealth; / one who desires liberation obtains liberation, fasting on Jayantī.
Those whose minds are intent on observing Jayantī, / even Yama ever fears them; they go to the supreme state.
Sūta said: / Having spoken to Nārada, he went as he had come; / and what I was asked by you, O brahmin sage, has also been related by me.
Those who hear the glorification of Jayantī with devotional disposition, / they too, freed from all sins, go to the supreme abode.
Those men who behold the reciter of the Purāṇa, O brahmin, / and likewise one who observes the Jayantī vow, even if sinful, go to the supreme state.

4.5.m: Śaunaka said: / Tell me, O wise one, by what action does a person become childless, / and by what [action], O Sūta, does a son come to be?
Sūta said: / This was formerly asked of Brahmā by the great-souled Nārada; / listen, O bull among sages, to what he said then.
Nārada said: / O Grandfather, of great wisdom, conversant with the ultimate meaning of all principles, / by what action, O lotus-born one, does a mortal become childless?
Or by what sin does a woman become barren? Before me / speak, as I listen, O you who are delighting in the welfare of all living beings!

By what action is a daughter born, or a eunuch? / By what does a man become one whose children die, and a woman one whose children die, exceedingly afflicted? / By what merit, O brahmin, does a son come to be again? Tell me!
Brahmā said: / I will tell you briefly; listen to that attentively! / You are asking about a matter that brings wonder to those who hear it.
A mortal who in a previous birth steals the livelihood of a brahmin / or causes it to be stolen, surely becomes childless in this world.
The mortal who in this life listens to the Purāṇa, / and endowed with faith gives land bearing crops,
a cow of many virtues, [or] a golden cow yielding much milk with a priestly gift, / and a golden image, surely obtains a son.
The woman who in a previous birth kills another's child / through deceit, surely becomes childless.
The woman who, endowed with faith, gives a golden image, / and drinks with devotion the water from a brahmin's feet,
and listens to the Purāṇa and gives abundant priestly gifts, / will have many children whose offspring live; there is no doubt about this.
A man who or a woman who, seeing a child drowning in water, does not rescue it, / surely becomes sonless, and she sonless, in this birth.
One should give a bull, a pumpkin with gold and with cloth, / as a gift to a brahmin, and should perform the auspicious vow for children.
He who gives a maiden named Gaurī [in marriage] and listens to the Purāṇa, / to him is born a son who destroys all sins.
The mortal who in a previous birth disappoints a guest, O twice-born one, / and inflicts punishment in anger, surely becomes childless.
One should reverently worship a brahmin and a guest, / give food and water, and likewise [build] an auspicious temple for God.
The woman who or the man who in a previous birth caused abortion, / she surely becomes one whose children die, and he one whose children die.
The woman who together with her husband observes the day of Hari / will have good sons and be cherished by her husband in every birth.
A man who takes cattle as wealth, or a Śūdra who deluded / abducts a brahmin woman, becomes a eunuch by that act.
One who commits this sin and afterward performs merit, / by the power of merit in this world a daughter is born, O twice-born one.
In the Tretā age there was a king named Śrīdhara, O twice-born one, / childless, wealthy; his wife was Hemaprabhāvatī.
Seeing Vyāsa arrive, who knew all the scriptures and wished the welfare of all people, / he asked: 'Why am I childless, O twice-born one?'
Having heard the king's words filled with humility, / seated upon the throne provided by the king, fashioned of gold and other [metals], he spoke.
The king and the queen, rejoiced, washed his feet, / and both drank the foot-washing water, which destroys all sins.
Vyāsa said: / Listen, O king, to what you asked, by which deed one is sonless; / this queen of yours is also sonless, and likewise follows the vow of devotion to one husband.
In your previous birth you were Candra, known by the name Varatanu; / your wife too, of fair limbs, was known by the name Śaṃkarī.
Once, while traveling on the road, seeing the son of a lowborn man drowning in water, / you two casually passed by, and he succumbed to death.
By the power of great merit, you two have become king and queen; / by the ripening of that deed, no son is born to you.
The king said: / By what merit may a son now be born, O lord? / Indeed, the life of men who are sonless is meaningless.
Vyāsa said: / Give a gift to a brāhmaṇa of a pumpkin together with cloth, and a bull accompanied by gold, / and likewise perform the observance for a child.
Give likewise a maiden of the Gaurī age [in marriage], and listen to the Purāṇa; / thereby a son will indeed be born, destroying all sins.
Brahmā said: / Having heard this, the king then offered the excellent gifts spoken by Vyāsa, / and, freed from sin, listened to the Purāṇa.
Then within a year a son was born, honored by all; / he became an emperor, a handsome leader of his family.
Sūta said: / Whoever hears this with devotion and makes an excellent gift, / if sonless, obtains a son; this has been told by me in brief.
And whatever woman, having listened with devotion, performs the worship of brāhmaṇas / according to the injunctions of the scriptures, O twice-born, will forever have a good son.
Whoever devotes gold, silver, cloth, / flower garlands, and sandalwood to the manuscript, [his act] destroys all sins.
That fool who in a previous birth was a slayer of a brāhmaṇa boy, / his son will be cruel for seven births, O twice-born.

4.6.m: Śaunaka said: / By what merit, O Sūta, is Vaikuṇṭha attained? / Tell me that as I listen; indeed, [it is] a boat on the ocean of worldly existence.
Sūta said: / Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, bringer of all auspiciousness! / I shall tell you in brief what destroys the sins of those who listen.
Whoever gives to Viṣṇu or to a brāhmaṇa a house built of clay, / hear the merit of that person, O best of the twice-born:
Freed from all sins, that brāhmaṇa will dwell in a palace / in the world of Viṣṇu forever, and is worshiped in Viṣṇu's realm.
Whoever gives a palatial house to Viṣṇu or to a brāhmaṇa / surely becomes a resident of heaven after attaining the abode of Hari.
In the end, going to the city of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million ancestors, O twice-born, / dwelling in a mansion of gold, he enjoys pleasures as he pleases.
As for the merit that arises from settling a brāhmaṇa, O sage, / even the Creator, the maker of all, is unable to calculate it.
The particles of dust can be counted, and rain drops can be counted, / but the fruit of providing a dwelling for a brāhmaṇa cannot be counted even by the Creator.
Long ago, Brahmā was questioned by Nārada about the origin of the worldly existence; / the Creator related it to him. Listen to that, O great sage.
Long ago, in the Dvāpara age, O brāhmaṇa, there was a very beautiful courtesan / with fine hair, eyes like a doe, a slender waist, and a charming smile.
Named Cañcalāpāṅgī, she once traveled to another country; / [though] endowed with all sins, which cast one into hell,
desiring [wealth] from an ocean of people by association, she went to a temple of God; / there she sat for a moment and chewed betel.
Having placed the remaining lime out of curiosity upon a depression on the wall of the temple, / she then went to the town in search of wealth, longing for a lover.
A rendezvous was hastily made by her with a certain lover; / having gone to the rendezvous in the forest at night, the courtesan became confused.
The merchant did not arrive at the rendezvous; looking about, she grew anxious: / 'Why has my beloved not come? Has he been devoured by serpents and tigers?
Why has he abandoned the meeting place? Has he gone, overwhelmed with passion? / Could he be yearning for another woman known to him?'
Reflecting on this within her heart, fearing the watchman, O twice-born, / she did not return to the city, since the public road was blocked by darkness.
In the meantime, a hungry tiger, capable of assuming any form at will, / sent by the god of Death, came forward and forcefully seized her, O twice-born.
Then the messengers of Yamuna's brother [Yama], raining dread, / their bodies like mountain peaks, arrived to lead her away on account of her sinful deeds.
Having crooked feet, crooked faces, raised noses, and many fangs, / taking leather ropes and clubs, to seize the unchaste woman, O twice-born,
the frenzied [messengers] bound the courtesan with ropes of leather. / Then, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, adorned with forest garlands,
sent by the God of gods, who is affectionate to his devotees, / resembling black clouds, with radiant lotus-like faces,
standing in ranks, with handsome noses, adorned with divine earrings, / the messengers of the noble Viṣṇu, moving along the path, saw [them].

The messengers of Viṣṇu said: / 'Who are you of deformed appearance, looking like demons? / Having taken this dearest of Viṣṇu's, this most excellent woman, where are you going?' / Having heard these words of theirs, they fled swiftly.
Then, filled with wrath, the messengers of Viṣṇu of great strength / struck down those couriers of Yama, the lord of the world.
With crowds of weapons such as the discus, radiant as ten million suns, / all the soldiers of Death fled weeping.
Terrified, they reported the entire event to Yama, O twice-born; / and Yama, having heard that story, spoke to Citragupta.
Dharma said: / 'By what merit, O minister, has the prostitute attained liberation? / Explain all this properly to me who is asking.'
Citragupta said: / 'She had accumulated very many sins from birth; / however, listen, O lord of the world, to the merit that is hers, if any exists.
Once, O Dharmarāja, the courtesan, adorned with all ornaments, / went swiftly to a certain city, desiring a lover and seeking wealth.
Staying in that temple of God there, she chewed betel, / and out of curiosity smeared the remaining lime on the wall.
By the power of that merit, the courtesan, freed from sins, / goes to Vaikuṇṭha, having escaped your punishment.'
Sūta said: / Having heard this speech, O twice-born, the messengers and Yama too / turned their minds to other duties, and that courtesan,
mounted upon a divine chariot yoked with royal swans, / surrounded by the attendants of Viṣṇu, went to the world of Viṣṇu.
By the command of the glorious Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million generations of her family, / she dwelt in a palace, O brāhmaṇa, and enjoyed various pleasures.
Whoever gives lime with devotion to the house of Hari with effort, / what merit might belong to him? I do not know, O foremost of the twice-born!
Whoever reads this chapter with devotion or listens to it with reverence, / completely freed from all sins, goes to the temple of Hari.

4.7.m:
Śaunaka said:
Tell me, O highly intelligent one, by what deed does one go to Goloka,
[and how] a person [crosses] from this ocean of worldly existence, so hard to cross, O wise one?
And tell the supreme glorification of Rādhā's eighth day, O Sūta.

Sūta said:
Nārada previously questioned Brahmā on this, O great sage.
Hear that in brief as he asked it, O twice-born.

Nārada said:
O grandfather, of great intellect, best among knowers of all scriptures!
Father, recount before me the eighth day of Rādhā's birth.

What is the fruit of its merit, or by whom was it performed formerly, O lord?
And for people who do not perform it, what sin would there be, O twice-born?

By what procedure should that vow be undertaken, and when?
And from what did that Rādhā originate? Tell me that from the very beginning.

Brahmā said:
O child, listen with full concentration to [the account of] the eighth day of Rādhā's birth.
I shall tell it in brief; in its entirety, [no one] except Hari

is able to declare that meritorious fruit, O Nārada.
Great sins accumulated over ten million births, such as killing a Brahmin,

perish for them instantly if they perform it even once with devotion.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by a thousand Ekādaśī days,

the merit of Rādhā's birth-eighth-day is a hundred times greater than that.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving gold equal [in weight] to Mount Meru,

by observing Rādhāṣṭamī even once, [the result is] a hundred times greater than that.
Whatever merit is attained by people through the gift of a thousand maidens in marriage,

that fruit is attained by people on the eighth day of Vṛṣabhānu's daughter.
And whatever fruit one might obtain by bathing in holy waters such as the Gaṅgā,

a human being obtains the fruit of the eighth day of Kṛṣṇa's life-breath-beloved.
Even a sinner who performs this vow, whether in jest or with faith,

goes to the abode of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million ancestors.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, O child, there was a fair woman, exceedingly lovely,

slender-waisted, fawn-eyed, of auspicious limbs, sweet-smiling,
with beautiful hair and lovely ears, known by the name Līlāvatī.

By her, many very grave sins were committed.
Once, wishing to seek [some] means [of enjoyment], she set out of her own accord from the city

and went to another city. There, seeing many wise people
devoted to the Rādhāṣṭamī vow in a beautiful temple of the deity,

worshipping the supreme image of Rādhā with devotional dispositions,
with fragrant scents, flowers, incenses, lamps, garments, and various kinds of fruits;

some were singing, some dancing, some reciting supreme praise,
and others joyfully playing cymbals, flutes, and drums—

seeing various persons of such sort, filled with curiosity,
she went near them and, endowed with humility, inquired:

“O virtuous souls! What are you doing with such joy?
Declare it, O meritorious ones, to me who am full of humility.”

Hearing her words, those Vaiṣṇavas intent on the welfare of others
and devoted to the vow then began to speak.

Those observing the vow of Rādhā said:
“Since Śrī Rādhikā was born on the bright eighth day in the month of Bhādra,
that eighth day has arrived today; we observe it with great diligence.

Sin arising from cow-slaughter, from theft, from killing a Brahmin,
and from the abduction of another's wife, as well as from violating the Guru's bed,

sin arising from breach of trust, and likewise that arising from killing a woman—
these are quickly destroyed for mortals when this eighth day is observed.”

Having heard their words which destroy all sins,
reflecting again and again, [she thought,] “I too shall observe it.”

Having observed that supreme vow right there together with the observers of the vow,
by fate she met her death from the bite of a snake, [now] purified.

Then, by Yama's order, messengers with nooses and clubs in hand
arrived to lead her away, and they bound her with great distress.

When they made up their minds to lead her to the abode of Yama,
then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing conch, discus, and mace,

and an auspicious golden celestial vehicle drawn by royal swans.
Quickly severing the nooses with the edges of their discuses,

they placed that woman, whose sins had departed, upon the chariot,
and they carried her to the charming city of Viṣṇu named Goloka.

There she stayed with Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā by the grace of the vow.
O child, whatever foolish-minded person does not observe the Rādhāṣṭamī vow,

there is no deliverance for him from hell even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
And whatever women do not observe this vow which bestows auspiciousness,

which brings pleasure to Rādhā and Viṣṇu, and destroys all sins,
in the end, going to the city of Yama, they fall into hell for a long time.

If ever they obtain a birth on earth, they certainly become widows.
Once upon a time, O child, the Earth, afflicted by hordes of wicked beings,

assuming the form of a cow, deeply distressed, came into my presence.
Weeping repeatedly, she reported her distress.

Hearing her words, I went into the presence of Viṣṇu;
and the heap of distress of the Earth was immediately reported to Kṛṣṇa.

By him it was said: “Go, O Brahmā, together with the gods to the surface of the earth;
I too shall go there later along with my attendants.”

Having heard that, accompanied by the gods, I came to the surface of the earth.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having summoned Rādhā, who is dearer to him than his own life,

spoke these words: “O goddess, I am going to the surface of the earth.
For the destruction of the burden of the earth, go you to the mortal world.”
Having heard this, that Rādhā also arrived on the earth, / in the month of Bhādra, in the bright fortnight, on the lunar day called the eighth.

She, Rādhikā, was born during the day on the sacrificial ground of Vṛṣabhānu;
and when it was being cleared for the sacrifice, she of divine form was seen.

The king, having become joyful upon finding her, took her to his own abode
and gave her to his queen, and she protected and raised her.
Thus has been related to you, child, the speech that was asked by you. / It is to be concealed, concealed, concealed with great effort.

Sūta said:
Whoever hears this with devotion, which bestows the fruit of the four aims of life,
freed from all sins, goes in the end to the home of Hari.

4.8.m:
Śaunaka said:
Why was the churning of the ocean previously performed by the immortals, O Sūta, O guru?
Curiosity has arisen in my heart to hear it; tell it.

Durvāsas, of great ascetic fervor and great splendor, born of a portion of Śiva,
a Brahmin sage, once went to heaven to see Indra.

At that time, he saw the husband of Śacī mounted upon an elephant.
Seeing him, the great sage gave him a garland of pārijāta flowers.

Having taken that garland and placed it on the head of the elephant,
the king of the gods, O Brahmin, proceeded toward Nandana with his army.

The elephant seized that garland, shredded it, and threw it down
upon the surface of the earth. Greatly angered, the great sage said to him:

“Since you, endowed with the sole fortune of the three worlds, treat me with contempt,
your fortune of the three worlds shall surely be destroyed, there is no doubt.”

Then Śakra went quickly back to his own city and fell asleep.
He saw that the mother of the worlds had vanished of her own accord.

When she had vanished, the three worlds were then ruined;
all [beings], afflicted with hunger and thirst, continuously cried out in distress.
The clouds did not rain, and the reservoirs dried up; / all the trees withered, devoid of fruit and flowers.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, all went into the presence of Brahmā; / they all related their grief and sorrow to the Grandfather.
Hearing the words of the gods, the Creator, together with the hosts of gods / and the sages headed by Bhṛgu, set out for the Ocean of Milk.
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, he worshiped Viṣṇu; / the Creator muttered the eight-syllabled mantra, meditating on the Lord of the universe.
Then the Blessed Lord, pleased with all the celestials, / mounted on the son of Vinatā, arrived, the compassionate Lord.
Seeing him dressed in yellow garments, four-armed, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / the Lord of the worlds, having eyes resembling lotuses,
Viṣṇu, the boat on the ocean of worldly existence, adorned with a forest garland, / his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha jewel, overflowed with tears of joy,

they praised him with cries of 'Victory!' and bowed down continually. / The Blessed Lord said: 'Choose a boon, O gods! Why have you come? / I am the giver of boons; tell me that, and I will give it to you without fail.'
The gods said: 'O compassionate one, by the curse of a brāhmaṇa, the three worlds are deprived of prosperity, / tormented by hunger and thirst, O Lord, together with gods, asuras, and humans.
Protect all these worlds; we have come to you for refuge.' / The Blessed Lord said: 'Indirā has disappeared on account of the curse of a brāhmaṇa, O gods.
By whose mere side-glance the world was endowed with sovereignty. / Therefore, O all you gods, having uprooted the golden mountain,
making Mount Mandara the churning rod wrapped around with the king of serpents, / you gods, together with the daityas, perform the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
From it Lakṣmī, the mother of the universe, will arise, O gods; / delighted by her, O fortunate ones, you will be [prosperous], without a doubt.
I myself will support the mountain on all sides in the form of a tortoise.' / Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished; / all the gods and asuras went to churn the ocean, O twice-born.
